Friendship and social life

How to support someone going through a hard time

You often do not need the perfect words. Listening, validating and offering concrete help is usually worth more than advice.

A friend has lost their job, a colleague is grieving or someone in your family is depressed. You want to help, but you do not know what to say and fear putting your foot in it. It is a very common situation.

What studies show

Not all support helps equally. In 2000, Niall Bolger and colleagues followed students preparing for a very demanding exam and their partners. Curiously, the most helpful support was the kind the person did not perceive as help, "invisible" support: being available, doing tasks without announcing it or listening without lecturing. Very visible support, by contrast, sometimes increased distress, perhaps because it conveyed that the person could not cope alone.

Other well-meant phrases often go down badly: "at least…", "everything happens for a reason" or "if I were you…". They minimise what the other person feels.

Support that goes unnoticed

Paradoxically, the most obvious help is sometimes not the most welcome. Niall Bolger found that people preparing for an important exam felt better on days when their partner helped without them noticing, for example by taking on household chores, than on days when they received explicit advice. Very visible support can make the person feel incapable or indebted.

Looking after the helper too

Supporting someone who is struggling for a long time is tiring. It is normal to feel frustrated or not know what else to do. It helps to share the support among several people, keep up your own activities and breaks, and encourage the person to seek professional help when distress goes on or is intense, without feeling that this means abandoning them. If thoughts of suicide appear, do not keep it secret: it is time to get help.

What usually helps

  • Listen more than you talk. Open questions such as "how are you coping?" leave room.
  • Validate: "it makes sense that you feel that way" helps more than trying to convince them it is not so bad.
  • Offer concrete help: "I'll bring dinner round on Thursday" works better than "let me know if you need anything".
  • Keep in touch beyond the first few weeks, when support often fades away.
  • Look after yourself too: supporting someone over a long period is tiring.
If the person talks about ending their life, take it seriously, ask them directly and help them seek help. Crisis lines (in Spain, 024) also support family and friends.

References

  1. Bolger, N., Zuckerman, A. y Kessler, R. C. (2000). Invisible support and adjustment to stress. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(6), 953–961.
  2. Rimé, B. (2009). Emotion elicits the social sharing of emotion. Emotion Review, 1(1), 60–85.
  3. Bolger, N., Zuckerman, A. y Kessler, R. C. (2000). Invisible support and adjustment to stress. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(6), 953–961.
